question: Did a defective Djehutihotep facsimile divert scientific effort into redundant or historically misdirected wet-sand friction research?

findings.claim: The 2014 Fall et al. sled-friction study was materially motivated in part by the Djehutihotep image tradition.
basis: The paper introduction opens with ancient Egyptian tomb drawings suggesting that wetting sand may influence sled friction.
Figure 1 identifies the front figure as pouring water onto sand.
The experimental PVC sled is described as having rounded edges 'as the Egyptian sled'.
The work was also situated in a broader friction/granular-transport research programme, so sole causation is not established.

findings.claim: The basic mechanical effects of small liquid fractions and capillary bridges in wet granular materials were already known before 2014.
basis: Wet granular capillary cohesion had a substantial pre-2014 literature, including reviews and direct shear experiments.
Fall et al. themselves state that the mechanical behavior of sand upon addition of small amounts of water was fully understood and tested for different grain materials and liquids.
Moller and Bonn (2007) measured an optimum wet-granular shear modulus at low liquid fraction; Pakpour et al. (2012) measured wet-sand modulus and optimum strength.

findings.claim: The specific 2014 result that partially wetting a sand bed can reduce sled sliding friction was already established and therefore redundant.
basis: Earlier friction studies examined different regimes, including fully immersed granular layers, humidity-conditioned layers, and dry granular sliders.

The 2014 paper explicitly notes earlier humidity/capillary reasoning that would predict increased rather than decreased friction, making its partially wetted sled result a narrower contribution not shown here to be duplicative.

findings.claim: The 2014 mechanistic explanation was later revised within the same research line.
basis: The 2014 paper linked reduced sliding friction roughly to increased shear elastic modulus.

Liefferink et al. (2020) state that because the sled plastically deforms/ploughs the sand, the linear elastic modulus is not the pertinent quantity and argue that penetration hardness controls the frictional response.

findings.claim: The water-lubrication historical interpretation is invalid because of the hand/rope geometric defect already detected.
basis: The current geometric trial tested hand position relative to skirt/rope geometry.
The water hypothesis materially depends on the separate visual claim that the front figure and represented material constitute deliberate wetting of the travel surface.
That feature must be independently compared between surviving wall, authenticated upstream images and derivative reconstructions before invalidation can propagate.

next_prosecution: Feature-scope image test of the front standing figure, vessel/stream, contact point and ground/sled relation in wall versus derivative.
Trace the exact image/plate used by Fall et al. back through Newberry and any Brown-derived source.
Audit pre-2014 literature for the exact partially wetted sled/ploughing configuration to determine novelty or redundancy at matching scope.
Map later citations that use laboratory success as confirmation of the Egyptian historical interpretation.
Seek documented research cost, funding, dissemination reach and downstream experimental replication before making an opportunity-cost or 'waste' finding.
